claim: Multispecies microbial communities (microbiomes) influence animal biology in diverse ways.
source: Multispecies microbial communities (microbiomes) influence animal biology in diverse ways (McFall-Ngai et al., 2013): microbiomes modulate disease (van Nood et al., 2013), metabolize nutrients (Zhu et al., 2011), synthesize vitamins (Degnan et al., 2014), and modify behavior (Bravo et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research demonstrating various effects of microbiomes on animal biology.

claim: Microbiomes modulate disease.
source: Multispecies microbial communities (microbiomes) influence animal biology in diverse ways (McFall-Ngai et al., 2013): microbiomes modulate disease (van Nood et al., 2013), metabolize nutrients (Zhu et al., 2011), synthesize vitamins (Degnan et al., 2014), and modify behavior (Bravo et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to van Nood et al., 2013.

claim: Microbiomes metabolize nutrients.
source: Multispecies microbial communities (microbiomes) influence animal biology in diverse ways (McFall-Ngai et al., 2013): microbiomes modulate disease (van Nood et al., 2013), metabolize nutrients (Zhu et al., 2011), synthesize vitamins (Degnan et al., 2014), and modify behavior (Bravo et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2011.

claim: Microbiomes synthesize vitamins.
source: Multispecies microbial communities (microbiomes) influence animal biology in diverse ways (McFall-Ngai et al., 2013): microbiomes modulate disease (van Nood et al., 2013), metabolize nutrients (Zhu et al., 2011), synthesize vitamins (Degnan et al., 2014), and modify behavior (Bravo et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Degnan et al., 2014.

claim: Microbiomes modify behavior.
source: Multispecies microbial communities (microbiomes) influence animal biology in diverse ways (McFall-Ngai et al., 2013): microbiomes modulate disease (van Nood et al., 2013), metabolize nutrients (Zhu et al., 2011), synthesize vitamins (Degnan et al., 2014), and modify behavior (Bravo et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bravo et al., 2011.

claim: Some aspects of microbial community function are the product of inter-species interactions.
source: Some aspects of microbial community function are the product of inter-species interactions (Rath and Dorrestein, 2012; Manor et al., 2014; Gerber, 2014; Gonzalez et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Microorganisms modulate the metabolomes of neighboring species.
source: For example, microorganisms modulate the metabolomes of neighboring species (Derewacz et al., 2015; Jarosz et al., 2014) and microbial metabolites (e.g., antibiotics) alter bacterial transcriptional responses (Goh et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Derewacz et al., 2015 and Jarosz et al., 2014.

claim: Microbial metabolites (e.g., antibiotics) alter bacterial transcriptional responses.
source: For example, microorganisms modulate the metabolomes of neighboring species (Derewacz et al., 2015; Jarosz et al., 2014) and microbial metabolites (e.g., antibiotics) alter bacterial transcriptional responses (Goh et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Goh et al., 2002.

claim: The Drosophila microbiome consists largely of yeasts, acetic acid bacteria, and lactic acid bacteria.
source: The Drosophila microbiome consists largely of yeasts, acetic acid bacteria, and lactic acid bacteria (Chandler et al., 2011, 2012; Broderick and Lemaitre, 2012; Camargo and Phaff, 1957; Staubach et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research on the Drosophila microbiome composition.

claim: Yeasts attract Drosophila via ester production.
source: Yeasts attract Drosophila via ester production (Christiaens et al., 2014; Schiabor et al., 2014), induce Drosophila egg-laying behavior (Becher et al., 2012), and are vital for larval development (Becher et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Christiaens et al., 2014 and Schiabor et al., 2014.

claim: Yeasts induce Drosophila egg-laying behavior.
source: Yeasts attract Drosophila via ester production (Christiaens et al., 2014; Schiabor et al., 2014), induce Drosophila egg-laying behavior (Becher et al., 2012), and are vital for larval development (Becher et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Becher et al., 2012.

claim: Yeasts are vital for larval development.
source: Yeasts attract Drosophila via ester production (Christiaens et al., 2014; Schiabor et al., 2014), induce Drosophila egg-laying behavior (Becher et al., 2012), and are vital for larval development (Becher et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Becher et al., 2012.

claim: Lactic and acetic acid bacteria produce metabolites (e.g., acids) that may repel Drosophila at high acid concentrations.
source: Lactic and acetic acid bacteria produce metabolites (e.g., acids) that may repel Drosophila at high acid concentrations, while also inducing egg-laying preference for sites containing acetic acid (Ai et al., 2010; Joseph et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ai et al., 2010 and Joseph et al., 2009.

claim: Lactic and acetic acid bacteria induce egg-laying preference for sites containing acetic acid.
source: Lactic and acetic acid bacteria produce metabolites (e.g., acids) that may repel Drosophila at high acid concentrations, while also inducing egg-laying preference for sites containing acetic acid (Ai et al., 2010; Joseph et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ai et al., 2010 and Joseph et al., 2009.

claim: Yeasts serve as food, providing Drosophila vitamins, sterols, and amino acids.
source: Yeasts serve as food, providing Drosophila vitamins, sterols, and amino acids (Broderick and Lemaitre, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Broderick and Lemaitre, 2012.

claim: Lactic and acetic acid bacteria are gut microbiome members.
source: Lactic and acetic acid bacteria are gut microbiome members (Wong et al., 2011) promoting larval development (Shin et al., 2011; Storelli et al., 2011), increasing resistance to pathogens (Blum et al., 2013), inducing intestinal stem cell proliferation (Buchon et al., 2009), and reducing adult sugar and lipid levels (Newell and Douglas, 2014; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wong et al., 2011.

claim: Lactic and acetic acid bacteria promote larval development.
source: Lactic and acetic acid bacteria are gut microbiome members (Wong et al., 2011) promoting larval development (Shin et al., 2011; Storelli et al., 2011), increasing resistance to pathogens (Blum et al., 2013), inducing intestinal stem cell proliferation (Buchon et al., 2009), and reducing adult sugar and lipid levels (Newell and Douglas, 2014; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shin et al., 2011 and Storelli et al., 2011.

claim: Lactic and acetic acid bacteria increase resistance to pathogens.
source: Lactic and acetic acid bacteria are gut microbiome members (Wong et al., 2011) promoting larval development (Shin et al., 2011; Storelli et al., 2011), increasing resistance to pathogens (Blum et al., 2013), inducing intestinal stem cell proliferation (Buchon et al., 2009), and reducing adult sugar and lipid levels (Newell and Douglas, 2014; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blum et al., 2013.

claim: Lactic and acetic acid bacteria induce intestinal stem cell proliferation.
source: Lactic and acetic acid bacteria are gut microbiome members (Wong et al., 2011) promoting larval development (Shin et al., 2011; Storelli et al., 2011), increasing resistance to pathogens (Blum et al., 2013), inducing intestinal stem cell proliferation (Buchon et al., 2009), and reducing adult sugar and lipid levels (Newell and Douglas, 2014; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buchon et al., 2009.

claim: Lactic and acetic acid bacteria reduce adult sugar and lipid levels.
source: Lactic and acetic acid bacteria are gut microbiome members (Wong et al., 2011) promoting larval development (Shin et al., 2011; Storelli et al., 2011), increasing resistance to pathogens (Blum et al., 2013), inducing intestinal stem cell proliferation (Buchon et al., 2009), and reducing adult sugar and lipid levels (Newell and Douglas, 2014; Wong et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Newell and Douglas, 2014 and Wong et al., 2014.

claim: Drosophila avoids 'green' fruit and is attracted to 'overripe' fruit.
source: Drosophila avoids 'green' fruit and is attracted to 'overripe' fruit (Turner and Ray, 2009), yet it is unclear how Drosophila behavior is influenced by the dynamic multispecies fruit microbiome and its metabolic properties.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Turner and Ray, 2009.

claim: When the strains were grown individually, Drosophila was strongly attracted to yeasts, moderately attracted to acetic acid bacteria, and neutral or slightly repelled by lactic acid bacteria.
source: When the strains were grown individually, Drosophila was strongly attracted to yeasts, moderately attracted to acetic acid bacteria, and neutral or slightly repelled by lactic acid bacteria (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Drosophila preferred microbial communities grown together to microorganisms grown individually and then mixed prior to analysis.
source: Drosophila preferred microbial communities grown together to microorganisms grown individually and then mixed prior to analysis (defined throughout as a separate-culture mixture, Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: When tested against apple juice medium (AJM), Drosophila attraction to the community was stronger than to the separate-culture mixture or individual members.
source: Focusing on a model Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Acetobacter malorum community, we found that when tested against apple juice medium (AJM), Drosophila attraction to the community was stronger than to the separate-culture mixture or individual members (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: When grown alone, S. cerevisiae and A. malorum had similar growth profiles.
source: When grown alone, the microorganisms had similar growth profiles (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When grown with A. malorum, S. cerevisiae populations first increased, then decreased between 60 and 72 hr, and were undetectable by 96 hr.
source: However, when grown with A. malorum, S. cerevisiae populations first increased, then decreased between 60 and 72 hr, and were undetectable by 96 hr (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Drosophila did not prefer the co-culture relative to the separate-culture mixture at 34 hr.
source: Drosophila did not prefer the co-culture relative to the separate-culture mixture at 34 hr; however, Drosophila was more attracted to the co-culture from 48–127 hr (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Drosophila was more attracted to the co-culture from 48–127 hr.
source: Drosophila did not prefer the co-culture relative to the separate-culture mixture at 34 hr; however, Drosophila was more attracted to the co-culture from 48–127 hr (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Drosophila attraction to the 96 hr co-culture was stronger than its preference for the 48, 54, or 60 hr co-cultures.
source: Moreover, the Drosophila attraction to the 96 hr co-culture was stronger than its preference for the 48, 54, or 60 hr co-cultures (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Drosophila preference for the co-culture correlated with lower pH and S. cerevisiae population density.
source: Drosophila preference for the co-culture correlated with lower pH and S. cerevisiae population density, despite Drosophila olfactory avoidance of acid (Ai et al., 2010) and reliance on yeast for nutrition (Anagnostou et al., 2010) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and 2D, and citations to Ai et al., 2010 and Anagnostou et al., 2010.

claim: Drosophila preference did not correlate with viable A. malorum populations.
source: Drosophila preference did not correlate with viable A. malorum populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Homozygous mutants of Drosophila ORCO and Or42b showed a significant reduction in attraction to the co-culture during the most attractive phase (67–115 hr).
source: During the most attractive phase of the co-culture (e.g. 67–115 hr), homozygous mutants of Drosophila ORCO and Or42b showed a significant reduction in attraction to the co-culture, whereas no role was detected for Drosophila homozygous mutants in several Irs or Or35a (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No role was detected for Drosophila homozygous mutants in several Irs or Or35a during the most attractive phase of the co-culture (67–115 hr).
source: During the most attractive phase of the co-culture (e.g. 67–115 hr), homozygous mutants of Drosophila ORCO and Or42b showed a significant reduction in attraction to the co-culture, whereas no role was detected for Drosophila homozygous mutants in several Irs or Or35a (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: As co-culture growth proceeded (e.g. 139–163 hr), attraction decreased and the role of Or42b and ORCO waned.
source: As co-culture growth proceeded (e.g. 139–163 hr), attraction decreased and the role of Or42b and ORCO waned (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: An independent homozygous mutant of ORCO also showed reduced attraction to the co-culture.
source: An independent homozygous mutant of ORCO also showed reduced attraction to the co-culture, whereas the heterozygotes ORCO/+ and Or42/+ were attracted to the co-culture similarly to wild-type flies (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The heterozygotes ORCO/+ and Or42/+ were attracted to the co-culture similarly to wild-type flies.
source: An independent homozygous mutant of ORCO also showed reduced attraction to the co-culture, whereas the heterozygotes ORCO/+ and Or42/+ were attracted to the co-culture similarly to wild-type flies (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ORCO is a required co-receptor for all other Or gene products.
source: ORCO is a required co-receptor for all other Or gene products (Larsson et al., 2004) and Or42b, one of the most conserved olfactory receptors, detects esters and 1,1-diethoxyethane (Mathew et al., 2013; Asahina et al., 2009; Stökl et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Larsson et al., 2004.

claim: Or42b, one of the most conserved olfactory receptors, detects esters and 1,1-diethoxyethane.
source: ORCO is a required co-receptor for all other Or gene products (Larsson et al., 2004) and Or42b, one of the most conserved olfactory receptors, detects esters and 1,1-diethoxyethane (Mathew et al., 2013; Asahina et al., 2009; Stökl et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mathew et al., 2013, Asahina et al., 2009, and Stökl et al., 2010.

claim: A non-ORCO factor explains ~40% of Drosophila co-culture preference.
source: Moreover, a non-ORCO factor explains ~40% of Drosophila co-culture preference (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: ORCO is fully responsible for the Drosophila attraction to apple cider vinegar.
source: Previous work found that ORCO is fully responsible for the Drosophila attraction to apple cider vinegar (Semmelhack and Wang, 2009), suggesting that the behavioral circuit activated by inter-species interactions between S. cerevisiae and A. malorum is distinct from the circuit activated by apple cider vinegar.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Semmelhack and Wang, 2009.

claim: The behavioral circuit activated by inter-species interactions between S. cerevisiae and A. malorum is distinct from the circuit activated by apple cider vinegar.
source: Previous work found that ORCO is fully responsible for the Drosophila attraction to apple cider vinegar (Semmelhack and Wang, 2009), suggesting that the behavioral circuit activated by inter-species interactions between S. cerevisiae and A. malorum is distinct from the circuit activated by apple cider vinegar.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of ORCO's role in apple cider vinegar attraction versus co-culture attraction, supported by citation to Semmelhack and Wang, 2009.

claim: Five co-culture volatiles (ethanol, isobutanol, isoamyl alcohol, acetic acid, isoamyl acetate) were confirmed with standards.
source: Five co-culture volatiles (ethanol, isobutanol, isoamyl alcohol, acetic acid, isoamyl acetate) were confirmed with standards (Table 1—source data 1 and 2) and quantified with standard curves (Table 1—source data 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1 and associated source data.

claim: The alcohol concentrations were lower in the co-culture relative to the other experimental groups.
source: The alcohol concentrations were lower, and acetic acid and isoamyl acetate were unique in the co-culture relative to the other experimental groups (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Acetic acid and isoamyl acetate were unique in the co-culture relative to the other experimental groups.
source: The alcohol concentrations were lower, and acetic acid and isoamyl acetate were unique in the co-culture relative to the other experimental groups (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: The dynamics of Drosophila co-culture preference mirrored ethanol depression and acetic acid accumulation in the co-culture.
source: Consistent with a relationship between ethanol catabolism, acetic acid anabolism, and Drosophila attraction, the dynamics of Drosophila co-culture preference mirrored ethanol depression and acetic acid accumulation in the co-culture (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: As ethanol catabolism and acetic acid anabolism proceeded (36–96 hr), Drosophila attraction toward the co-culture increased until 96 hr, at which point it decreased.
source: Furthermore, as ethanol catabolism and acetic acid anabolism proceeded (36–96 hr), Drosophila attraction toward the co-culture increased until 96 hr, at which point it decreased, consistent with lower turnover of ethanol at the end of ethanol catabolism (Figure 4A, black line).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Drosophila preferred the co-culture in the middle stage of ethanol catabolism to earlier or later stages of ethanol catabolism.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, Drosophila preferred the co-culture in the middle stage of ethanol catabolism to earlier or later stages of ethanol catabolism (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Co-cultures using either A. malorum or A. pomorum wild-type (WT) along with S. cerevisiae were equally attractive to Drosophila.
source: Co-cultures using either A. malorum or A. pomorum wild-type (WT) along with S. cerevisiae were equally attractive to Drosophila (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Drosophila preferred the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT versus a separate-culture mixture.
source: Drosophila preferred the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT versus a separate-culture mixture; however, Drosophila did not prefer the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA versus a separate-culture mixture (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Drosophila did not prefer the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA versus a separate-culture mixture.
source: Drosophila preferred the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT versus a separate-culture mixture; however, Drosophila did not prefer the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA versus a separate-culture mixture (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Drosophila preferred the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT to the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA.
source: Moreover, Drosophila preferred the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT to the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ethanol catabolism is necessary for Drosophila to discriminate between the co-culture and the separate-culture mixture.
source: In sum, ethanol catabolism is necessary for Drosophila to discriminate between the co-culture and the separate-culture mixture.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results showing that the adhA mutant, which cannot catabolize ethanol, eliminates Drosophila preference for the co-culture.

claim: Acetic acid, six acetate esters, an acetaldehyde metabolic derivative (acetoin), a putative acetaldehyde metabolic derivative (2,4,5-trimethyl-1,3-dioxolane), and two unknown metabolites were more abundant in the co-culture relative to the separate-culture mixture or co-culture with A. pomorum adhA.
source: Acetic acid, six acetate esters, an acetaldehyde metabolic derivative (acetoin), a putative acetaldehyde metabolic derivative (2,4,5-trimethyl-1,3-dioxolane), and two unknown metabolites were more abundant in the co-culture relative to the separate-culture mixture or co-culture with A. pomorum adhA (Table 2, Table 2—source data 1–6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2 and associated source data.

claim: Esters and acetic acid, but not esters alone, were sufficient to fully restore the attractiveness of the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA to the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT levels.
source: To determine the molecular basis for Drosophila co-culture preference, select metabolites were added to the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA. Esters and acetic acid, but not esters alone, were sufficient to fully restore the attractiveness of the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA to the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT levels (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Acetoin was moderately increased in the co-culture compared with the separate-culture mixture.
source: Consistent with this idea, acetoin was moderately increased in the co-culture compared with the separate-culture mixture (Table 2—source data 1); strikingly, acetoin was increased ~27 fold in the tri-culture (S. cerevisiae, A. malorum, and L. plantarum) compared to the co-culture (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and was attractive to Drosophila (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 2—source data 1.

claim: Acetoin was increased ~27 fold in the tri-culture (S. cerevisiae, A. malorum, and L. plantarum) compared to the co-culture.
source: Consistent with this idea, acetoin was moderately increased in the co-culture compared with the separate-culture mixture (Table 2—source data 1); strikingly, acetoin was increased ~27 fold in the tri-culture (S. cerevisiae, A. malorum, and L. plantarum) compared to the co-culture (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and was attractive to Drosophila (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, 5B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Acetoin was attractive to Drosophila.
source: Consistent with this idea, acetoin was moderately increased in the co-culture compared with the separate-culture mixture (Table 2—source data 1); strikingly, acetoin was increased ~27 fold in the tri-culture (S. cerevisiae, A. malorum, and L. plantarum) compared to the co-culture (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and was attractive to Drosophila (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Even at the lowest tested levels, acetaldehyde supplementation stimulated the separate-culture mixture to attractiveness levels equal to the co-culture.
source: Even at the lowest tested levels, acetaldehyde supplementation stimulated the separate-culture mixture to attractiveness levels equal to the co-culture (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Three acetaldehyde metabolic derivatives—acetoin, 1,1-diethoxyethane (an acetal), and 2,3-butanedione—were sufficient to induce the attractiveness of the separate-culture mixture to levels equivalent to the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT.
source: Three acetaldehyde metabolic derivatives—acetoin, 1,1-diethoxyethane (an acetal), and 2,3-butanedione—were sufficient to induce the attractiveness of the separate-culture mixture to levels equivalent to the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT using concentrations of each metabolite at or below the physiological concentration of acetoin found in the tri-culture (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A pure metabolite mixture comprised of key metabolic groups produced by microbial communities attracted Drosophila similarly to the co-culture.
source: A pure metabolite mixture comprised of key metabolic groups produced by microbial communities and identified in this study (esters, acetaldehyde metabolic derivatives, alcohols, acid) attracted Drosophila similarly to the co-culture (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The acetaldehyde metabolic derivatives alone were sufficient to attract Drosophila similarly to the co-culture.
source: Interestingly, the acetaldehyde metabolic derivatives alone were sufficient to attract Drosophila similarly to the co-culture (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Removal of the acetaldehyde metabolic derivatives group alone reduced Drosophila attraction.
source: Moreover, removal of the acetaldehyde metabolic derivatives group alone reduced Drosophila attraction (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Adult Drosophila survival was highest when given metabolites associated with middle-staged ethanol catabolism compared with pre- or end-stage ethanol catabolism.
source: Adult Drosophila survival was highest when given metabolites associated with middle-staged ethanol catabolism compared with pre- or end-stage ethanol catabolism (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Drosophila preferred to lay eggs in the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT to the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA.
source: Drosophila preferred to lay eggs in the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT to the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Larvae develop more slowly when consuming the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT compared with the co-culture containing A. pomomrum adhA.
source: In contrast, we found that larvae develop more slowly when consuming the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT compared with the co-culture containing A. pomomrum adhA (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A. pomorum WT kills the nutritious yeast cells, whereas the A. pomorum adhA mutant does not.
source: This result may be explained by the fact that A. pomorum WT kills the nutritious yeast cells, whereas the A. pomorum adhA mutant does not (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Drosophila laid significantly more eggs in the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT than the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA.
source: We found that Drosophila laid significantly more eggs in the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT than the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Following open-air exposure to environmental microbes, unidentified fungi grew on the co-cultures containing A. pomorum adhA, but did not grow on the co-cultures containing A. pomorum WT.
source: Following open-air exposure to environmental microbes, unidentified fungi grew on the co-cultures containing A. pomorum adhA, but did not grow on the co-cultures containing A. pomorum WT (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: More pupae and adults survived in the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT compared to the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA.
source: Furthermore, more pupae and adults survived in the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT compared to the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E and 7F.

claim: Emergent properties of a microbial community—volatile profile, population dynamics, and pH—influence Drosophila attraction, survival, and egg-laying behaviors.
source: Here, we have demonstrated how emergent properties of a microbial community—volatile profile, population dynamics, and pH—influence Drosophila attraction, survival, and egg-laying behaviors.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: This study is the first to identify the consequences of microbe-microbe metabolic exchange on animal behavior.
source: Our study is the first to identify the consequences of microbe-microbe metabolic exchange on animal behavior and discovers additional microbial interactions that attract Drosophila for further mechanistic study (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is an assertion by the authors about the novelty of their work.

claim: Microbe-microbe metabolic exchange generates unique and quantitatively different volatiles from those resulting from individual microbial metabolism.
source: Microbe-microbe metabolic exchange generates unique and quantitatively different volatiles from those resulting from individual microbial metabolism (Table 1 and 2, Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1, Table 2, and Figure 8.

claim: Acetobacter-generated acetate coupled to Saccharomyces-derived alcohols spawn diverse acetate esters.
source: Acetobacter-generated acetate coupled to Saccharomyces-derived alcohols spawn diverse acetate esters (Table 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1 and Table 2.

claim: The community of S. cerevisiae, A. malorum, and L. plantarum emitted higher levels of acetoin and attracted Drosophila more strongly than the co-culture of S. cerevisiae and A. malorum.
source: The community of S. cerevisiae, A. malorum, and L. plantarum emitted higher levels of acetoin and attracted Drosophila more strongly than the co-culture of S. cerevisiae and A. malorum (Figure 1D, Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 5.

claim: Acetoin and 2,3-butanedione are formed by an α-acetolactate intermediate in bacteria and directly from acetaldehyde in yeast.
source: Acetoin and 2,3-butanedione are formed by an α-acetolactate intermediate in bacteria and directly from acetaldehyde in yeast (Chuang et al., 1968).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chuang et al., 1968.

claim: S. cerevisiae produced low quantities of esters when grown alone in apple juice medium.
source: In this study, we found that S. cerevisiae produced low quantities of esters when grown alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nitrogen content positively correlates with yeast ester production.
source: Nitrogen content positively correlates with the yeast ester production (Becher et al., 2012; Rollero et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Becher et al., 2012 and Rollero et al., 2015.

claim: Drosophila attraction toward the co-culture increases as yeast viability declines.
source: However, we find that Drosophila attraction toward the co-culture increases as yeast viability declines (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Non-Saccharomyces Drosophila microbiome members also make ethanol.
source: Non-Saccharomyces Drosophila microbiome members also make ethanol (Ruyters et al., 2015) and diverse acetic acid bacteria catabolize ethanol, generalizing our findings to other microbial community combinations.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ruyters et al., 2015.

claim: Diverse acetic acid bacteria catabolize ethanol.
source: Non-Saccharomyces Drosophila microbiome members also make ethanol (Ruyters et al., 2015) and diverse acetic acid bacteria catabolize ethanol, generalizing our findings to other microbial community combinations.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about acetic acid bacteria.

claim: Ethanol can have deleterious or beneficial fitness consequences for Drosophila depending on concentration.
source: Ethanol can have deleterious or beneficial fitness consequences for Drosophila depending on concentration (Ranganathan et al., 1987; Azanchi et al., 2013) and ecological context (Kacsoh et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ranganathan et al., 1987, Azanchi et al., 2013, and Kacsoh et al., 2013.

claim: Juice agar plates inoculated with the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT had fewer viable yeast cells and larvae developed more slowly.
source: On the one hand, we observed that juice agar plates inoculated with the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT had fewer viable yeast cells and larvae developed more slowly, likely due to the lower vital nutrients (e.g. protein, vitamins) than would be available in the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: When exposed to environmental microbes, juice agar plates inoculated with the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT were not invaded by fungi, whereas the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA was susceptible to fungal growth.
source: On the other hand, when exposed to environmental microbes, juice agar plates inoculated with the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT were not invaded by fungi, whereas the co-culture containing A. pomorum adhA was susceptible to fungal growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Acetic acid inhibits phytopathogenic fungi.
source: Additionally, acetic acid, a unique metabolite in the co-culture containing A. pomorum WT, inhibits phytopathogenic fungi (Kang et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kang et al., 2003.

claim: Drosophila possesses specific and regionalized gut immune responses to the microbiome.
source: Drosophila possesses specific and regionalized gut immune responses to the microbiome (Lhocine et al., 2008; Ryu et al., 2008; Paredes et al., 2011; Costechareyre et al., 2016) implying a tolerant environment in which privileged microbiome members are maintained and reproduce in the Drosophila intestine.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lhocine et al., 2008, Ryu et al., 2008, Paredes et al., 2011, and Costechareyre et al., 2016.

claim: Drosophila acquires its adult microbiome from exogenous sources.
source: Other work suggests that Drosophila acquires its adult microbiome from exogenous sources, that adult microbiome abundance drops without continuous ingestion of exogenous microorganisms, and that the microbiome can be shaped by diet (Chandler et al., 2011; Blum et al., 2013; Broderick et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chandler et al., 2011, Blum et al., 2013, and Broderick et al., 2014.

claim: The Drosophila olfactory system is tuned to fruity (e.g., esters) and buttery (several acetaldehyde metabolic derivatives, such as 2,3-butanedione) smelling metabolites promoted by microbe-microbe interactions.
source: In sum, our results support a model in which the Drosophila olfactory system is tuned to fruity (e.g., esters) and buttery (several acetaldehyde metabolic derivatives, such as 2,3-butanedione) smelling metabolites promoted by microbe-microbe interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: adhA encodes pyrroloquinoline quinone-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase (PQQ-ADH-I), the enzyme that converts yeast-derived ethanol into acetaldehyde on path to acetic acid.
source: To test directly whether ethanol catabolism underpinned Drosophila co-culture preference, we evaluated Drosophila preference for the co-culture harboring a mutant in adhA, which encodes pyrroloquinoline quinone-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase (PQQ-ADH-I), the enzyme that converts yeast-derived ethanol into acetaldehyde on path to acetic acid (Shin et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Shin et al., 2011.
